questions.question: Q1
questions.text: List two properties of good algorithm.
questions.answer: Any two of the lecture's list: be correct; be unambiguous; give the correct solution for all cases; be simple; must terminate.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: What is the main purpose of analysis of algorithms?
questions.answer: To predict resource usage (mainly running time, also memory) as the input grows, so algorithms can be compared and their growth of run time predicted independently of hardware.

questions.question: Q1
questions.trap: j is set to 0 once, outside the for loop, so the while body runs only while i = 0 (6 times in total); later iterations do one failing test. Students who multiply 6 by (n+1) get the wrong count; the order is still linear.
questions.text:
Analyze the running time of the following program fragment assuming a RAM model of computation.
  j <- 0
  for i <- 0 to n
     while j <= 5
        j <- j + 1
questions.answer: With the slide-23 convention (1 step per assignment/comparison/addition; 'for i <- 0 to n' costs (n+2) assignments, (n+2) comparisons, (n+1) additions): j<-0 = 1; for control = 3n+5; while tests = 7 (when i = 0) + n (once per later i) = n+7; body runs 6 times in total = 12. T(n) = 4n + 25 = O(n).
questions.note: Lecture slides 24 and 25 show both versions (j reset inside the loop vs outside): the lecturer tests whether students notice where the initialisation sits.

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: What are the best case and worst case running time (in Big O notation) of the insertion sorting algorithm? When do you get such situations?
questions.answer: Best case O(n): input already sorted (the while test fails at once for every j). Worst case O(n^2): input in reverse order (every key is shifted past all earlier elements).

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Illustrate the operations of the Insertion sort algorithm for A = [10, 0, 8, 4] (assign the values only once to the given algorithm codes, then use a diagrammatic way). INSERTION-SORT pseudo-code is printed with the question.

questions.question: Q1
questions.topic: Big-O of a sum of terms
questions.trap: (b) Students pick n^20 because of the big coefficient, or 2^n because it is the first exponential they see.
questions.text: Find the Big oh value for (a) T(n) = log n + n + 100, (b) T(n) = 200n^20 + 100n^10 + 2^n + 3^n + n + 1. Justify your answer.
questions.answer: (a) O(n): n dominates log n and the constant (T(n) <= 3n for n >= 100). (b) O(3^n): 3^n grows faster than 2^n and any polynomial; coefficients 200, 100 are irrelevant (T(n)/3^n -> 1).

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: pow(x, n) = x^n = x * x^(n-1). Write a recursive relation for pow(x, n) (n non-negative integer). Clearly define the initial condition(s).
questions.answer: pow(x, n) = 1 if n = 0 (initial condition); pow(x, n) = x * pow(x, n-1) if n > 0.
questions.note: 7a-7c share one printed total of 6 marks (stored on 7a).

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Write a recursive algorithm in pseudo code for the above recursive relation.
questions.answer:
POW(x, n)
1 if n = 0
2    then return 1
3    else return x * POW(x, n - 1)

questions.question: Q1
questions.text: Write a recurrence equation that describes the running time T(n) of the part (b) algorithm.
questions.answer: T(0) = c1; T(n) = T(n-1) + c2 for n > 0 (one test, one multiplication, one return per call). Solving by repeated substitution: T(n) = c1 + n*c2 = O(n).

questions.question: Q2
questions.trap: The pivot is the LAST element (8), not the first; indices are 1-based. Sub-arrays of size 1 or 0 make no PARTITION call.
questions.text: QUICKSORT / PARTITION (x <- A[r]) are given. Illustrate the operations of QUICKSORT(A, p, r) for A = [28, 15, 1, 30, 0, 8].

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: What kinds of partitioning generate the best or worst case of quicksort?
questions.answer: Best: every PARTITION splits the array into two halves of (about) n/2 each -> O(n lg n). Worst: every split is 0 and n-1 elements (e.g. already sorted input with pivot = A[r]) -> O(n^2).

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: Write recurrence equations for the best case.
questions.answer: T(1) = c; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn for n > 1 (two half-size calls plus linear PARTITION).
questions.note: c and d share one printed total of 5 marks (stored on d).

questions.question: Q2
questions.text: Use the repeated substitution method to solve the best case recurrence equation.
questions.answer: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn = 4T(n/4) + 2cn = 8T(n/8) + 3cn = ... = 2^k T(n/2^k) + k*cn. Put n = 2^k (k = lg n): T(n) = nT(1) + cn lg n = cn + cn lg n = O(n lg n).

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Briefly describe (a) leaf node, (b) binary tree.
questions.answer: (a) A node with no children. (b) A tree in which every node has at most two children (left and right).
questions.note: Question three is printed twice in the paper (once as 'Question One' with items 7-12).

questions.question: Q3
questions.text: Prove that for a full binary tree with n nodes and height h, n + 1 = 2^(h+1).
questions.answer: A full binary tree has 2^i nodes on level i (i = 0..h). n = sum_{i=0..h} 2^i = 2^(h+1) - 1 (geometric series), so n + 1 = 2^(h+1).

questions.trap: BUILD_HEAP starts at i = floor(n/2) = 4 and goes DOWN to 1; it is not 8 successive insertions. After each exchange heap_size shrinks, so sorted tail elements are never compared again.

questions.question: Q3
questions.trap: The top three levels look perfect; the single violation is at the bottom (index 4 vs 9). Students who only check the root say 'yes'.
questions.text: Is <23, 17, 14, 6, 13, 10, 1, 5, 7, 12> a max heap? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: No. A[4] = 6 has right child A[9] = 7 > 6, violating A[parent(i)] >= A[i]. Every other parent-child pair satisfies the property.

questions.question: Q3
questions.trap: Students associate 'priority 1 = first' and answer min-heap; the stem says high number = high priority.
questions.text: CPU scheduling uses a priority queue where a higher number means higher priority. What type of heap should implement it?
questions.answer: A max-heap: the highest-priority (largest number) process is always at the root, so EXTRACT-MAX gives the next process in O(lg n).

questions.question: Q4
questions.topic: Draw a directed graph from (V, E)
questions.note: Graph representation/DFS is not in the nine lecture decks; graph vocabulary is reused in L07 (spanning trees).

questions.question: Q4
questions.text: Briefly explain the two methods to represent a graph. Which suits a sparse graph? Justify.
questions.answer: Adjacency matrix: |V| x |V| array, entry 1 (or the weight) if (u,v) in E; Theta(V^2) space. Adjacency list: an array of |V| lists holding each vertex's neighbours; Theta(V + E) space. Sparse graph (|E| much less than |V|^2): adjacency list, because it stores only existing edges.

questions.question: Q4

questions.answer: With alphabetical adjacency lists: a 1/12, b 2/7, c 3/4, d 5/6, e 8/11, f 9/10; tree edges (a,b), (b,c), (b,d), (a,e), (e,f).
questions.note: Flaw: adjacency-list order is not stated, so several discovery orders are defensible. Topic is outside the nine lectures.

questions.question: C
questions.text: What is meant by fixed length coding in data representation? Give one example.
questions.answer: Every symbol gets a codeword of the same length (ceil(log2 n) bits for n symbols). Examples: ASCII (8 bits), Unicode (16 bits).
questions.note: This 12-mark compression section has no question number in the paper; its parts are lettered e-h.

questions.question: C
questions.text: Digits 0-5 have frequencies 121, 50, 203, 401, 8, 195. Construct the codewords with the Huffman algorithm given at the end of the paper.

questions.question: C
questions.trap: Students give the bits per codeword, or use the fixed-length total.
questions.text: How many bits are needed to represent the digits in the file?
questions.answer: Huffman: sum f*len = 2166 bits (fixed-length would need 3 x 978 = 2934; entropy bound 2.111 bits/symbol = 2064.7 bits).

questions.question: C
questions.text: Construct the codewords for the same data using the Shannon-Fano algorithm.
questions.note: Flaw: the paper says the Shannon-Fano algorithm is 'at the end of the paper (page 16)' but the appendix does not contain it.

questions.question: C
questions.trap: Students answer 'Huffman' without computing; for this data the two totals are equal.
questions.text: Which codeword is optimal out of the codewords constructed by Huffman and Shannon-Fano?
questions.answer: Both cost 2166 bits for this file, so both are optimal here. In general only Huffman is guaranteed optimal; Shannon-Fano can be worse.

questions.question: Q5
questions.text: What is meant by optimal substructure in Dynamic Programming?
questions.answer: A problem has optimal substructure when an optimal solution contains within it optimal solutions to its sub-problems.

questions.question: Q5
questions.text: Construct a table for the 0/1 knapsack problem n = 4, c = 10, w = [3, 4, 6, 3], p = [6, 12, 8, 2] using the recursive solution given at the end of the paper.

questions.question: Q5
questions.trap: P(i,k) uses items i..n (the suffix). P(3,9) may use only items 3 and 4; students who use items 1..3 get 18.
questions.text: Find P(3,9) and P(1,10) using the recursive equations.

questions.question: Q5
questions.text: Briefly explain how you achieved the final solution.
questions.answer: Start at P(1,10); for each i, if P(i,k) = P(i+1,k) item i is left out, otherwise it is taken and k drops by w_i. Optimal subsets: [2, 3]; [1, 2, 4] (both profit 20).
questions.note: Flaw: this instance has TWO optimal subsets because P(1,10) ties (20 = 6 + 14). A mock instance must have a unique optimum.
